Regional Overview

This volume includes all countries whose region field in the Λ¹² v2 raw data is Northern Europe, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, Southern Europe, or Island Regions. The first 12 countries are primary targets accompanied by narrative briefings due to high volatility or interest (selection is tentative and subject to final confirmation by the author), while the remaining 33 countries constitute the data edition arranged in η ranking order. All chapters follow the standard format of Section 5.2 in Vol. 1.

Reference date 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Prior Trajectory

Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, operations have continued under a wartime economy, expanded defense spending, and a response framework against Western sanctions. Since the Ministry of Defense announced 5,937 military deaths in September 2022, no official casualty figures have been released, and the disclosure of demographic and mortality statistics has also been curtailed since 2025.

Current Administration's Direction

The administration maintains the position that the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from Donbas (the remaining territory of Donetsk) serves as a prerequisite for cessation of hostilities in US-mediated negotiations. Domestically, the direction is shifting toward strengthening state control over the information space, including blocking/throttling WhatsApp and Telegram and mandating the distribution of the state-run messenger 'Max'. The Central Bank progressively cut the key interest rate across 2025–2026, freezing it at 14% in September 2026.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-08-15A Trump-Putin summit was held in Anchorage, USA, but concluded without a ceasefire or peace agreement.[3]
  • 2026-02-12Authorities attempted a blanket ban on WhatsApp and tightened access restrictions on Telegram.[8]
  • 2026-02US-mediated negotiations halted after late February (US special envoys redirected to mediate the Iran war).[1]
  • 2026-05-07Presidential aide Ushakov stated that further negotiations are pointless until Ukrainian forces withdraw from Donbas.[1]
  • 2026-05-08A 3-day ceasefire announced by President Trump was maintained through May 10, with both sides alleging violations.[2]
  • 2026-09-05President Putin met with US special envoys Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow for over 3 hours, but no breakthrough was announced.[4]
  • 2026-09-11The Bank of Russia froze the key interest rate at 14% and projected 2026 inflation at 6–7%.[6]
  • 2026-09-18The first State Duma elections since the full-scale invasion took place (September 18–20); United Russia retained a majority with roughly 57% of party-list votes, while Yabloko had its candidate registrations canceled in advance.[5]

Public Trends

During the 2026 State Duma election period, independent monitoring platforms logged over 900 incident reports, including restrictions on observer access. Amid messenger bans and mandatory adoption of state-run messaging apps, some military personnel were reported to have expressed discontent over Telegram bandwidth throttling. No large-scale street collective actions regarding the war were reported within the scope of review (2025–2026 news agency and independent media coverage).

Discrepancies in Figures

Military deaths: The Russian Defense Ministry's last official announcement reported 5,937 as of 2022-09-21, with no subsequent updates. Independent outlets Mediazona and BBC Russian tallied 258,989 individually identified deaths as of 2026-09 (roughly 253,000 higher than the official announcement, explicitly noting the actual toll is likely higher). The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine claimed 1,528,970 Russian military personnel losses (total killed, wounded, missing, captured) as of 2026-09-27 (belligerent party figure). Economy: The IMF projected 2026 GDP growth at 1.1% (April 2026 forecast).

Data Notice

The Federal State Statistics Service of Russia (Rosstat) discontinued publishing regional monthly birth and death statistics in March 2025 and nationwide statistics in May 2025. The Defense Ministry has not made domestic military losses public since September 2022. Election result percentages show slight variations across reports depending on ballot counting progress (57.2–57.8%).

4. Current Situation Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateVolodymyr Zelensky2019-05 (Elections postponed under martial law)Servant of the People
Head of GovernmentSerhii Koretskyi2026-07-16Unconfirmed

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the reference list below.

Prior Trajectory

Since the full-scale invasion in 2022, operations have centered on national defense and securing external assistance under martial law. In July 2025, the Yulia Svyrydenko cabinet was inaugurated, and although legislation weakening the independence of anti-corruption agencies was passed that same year, it was restored within a week following protests. In November 2025, amid an investigation into alleged kickbacks at state-owned nuclear enterprise Energoatom, Head of the Office of the President Yermak resigned.

Current Government Direction

Following the inauguration of the Koretskyi cabinet in July 2026, policy is shifting toward fostering defense industries, preparing for the winter heating season, supporting frontline areas, and sustaining European integration as priorities, while restructuring foreign policy into a portfolio-specific dedicated envoy system. In negotiations, it maintains the stance of demanding a ceasefire along current contact lines with security guarantees, while refusing demands to withdraw from Donbas.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-07-22Parliament passed Law 12414 placing anti-corruption agencies (NABU and SAPO) under the Prosecutor General, signed by the president on the same day.[5]
  • 2025-07-31Following nationwide protests, parliament restored the independence of anti-corruption agencies by a 331–0 vote.[5]
  • 2025-11-28Amid an investigation into approximately $100 million in alleged Energoatom kickbacks ('Operation Midas'), Head of the Office of the President Andriy Yermak resigned.[6]
  • 2026-02-04President Zelensky announced confirmed Ukrainian military combat fatalities at 55,000.[7]
  • 2026-05-08A US-mediated three-day ceasefire (until May 10) went into effect, but both sides alleged violations.[8]
  • 2026-07-12Prime Minister Svyrydenko resigned following the president's announcement of a cabinet reshuffle.[3]
  • 2026-07-16The Verkhovna Rada appointed Serhii Koretskyi as Prime Minister with 289 votes in favor.[4]
  • 2026-07The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission recorded 437 civilian deaths in July, the highest monthly toll since May 2022.[2]
  • 2026-09-06US special envoys Witkoff and Kushner met with President Zelensky in Kyiv the day after talks in Moscow; airstrikes against both capitals were temporarily paused from September 5 to 8.[9][10]

Public Trends

Between July 23 and 30, 2025, despite restrictions on assemblies under martial law, large-scale protests broke out in major cities opposing the curtailment of anti-corruption agency independence, prompting the government to reverse the legislation within a week. Presidential and parliamentary elections remain postponed due to martial law. Within the verified scope for 2026 (news wire and Ukrainian press reports), no subsequent nationwide anti-government protests have been reported.

Discrepancies in Figures

Civilian casualties: According to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU), cumulative casualties from 2022-02-24 to 2026-07 stand at a minimum of 16,874 dead and 51,173 wounded (verified minimums), with 1,396 dead and 7,978 wounded in the first half of 2026 (a 37% increase compared to the first half of 2025). Military fatalities: Official Ukrainian government figures state 55,000 (2026-02, presidential announcement, excluding missing personnel). Russian claims regarding Ukrainian military losses cannot be verified. Russian military casualties: The Ukrainian General Staff claimed 1,528,970 casualties (total dead and wounded) as of 2026-09-27, whereas independent outlets Mediazona and the BBC confirmed 258,989 dead by name; the two counts differ in counting criteria. Economy: The IMF projected a 2026 growth rate of 2% (revised downward from 4.5% projected in 2025-10).

Data Caution

Because UN figures include only individually verified cases, they represent minimums; fatalities in Russian-occupied regions in the first half of 2026 were tallied separately at 94. Under wartime martial law, certain statistics such as military losses are not released periodically.

4. Current Situation Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateAna Brnabić — Acting President (President of the National Assembly)2026-09-28Serbian Progressive Party (SNS)
Head of GovernmentĐuro Macut2025-04-16Independent (Nominated by SNS-led ruling coalition)

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the reference list below.

Prior Trajectory

President Aleksandar Vučić and the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have dominated the political landscape since 2012. Following the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse (16 deaths) on November 1, 2024, university-student-led anti-corruption protests ensued, leading to the resignation of Prime Minister Miloš Vučević in January 2025. In April 2025, endocrinology professor Macut, who had no prior political background, was elected prime minister and pledged the normalization of schools and universities.

Current Government Direction

The government is shifting toward easing tensions via early elections, moving the parliamentary elections originally scheduled for December 2027 forward to October 25, 2026. President Vučić resigned on September 27, 2026—approximately eight months before the end of his term—to pursue a bid for prime minister, and early presidential elections must be held by late 2026.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2024-11-01A concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station collapsed, killing 16 people.[1]
  • 2025-01-28Prime Minister Vučević resigned following an assault on student protesters by ruling party members.[1]
  • 2025-03-15A large-scale anti-government protest was held in Belgrade (size estimates vary by source).[2]
  • 2025-04-16Parliament approved the Macut cabinet with 153 votes in favor.[1]
  • 2026-05-24Clashes broke out with police in Belgrade during a student-led protest demanding early general elections, and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights expressed concerns over attacks on journalists and protesters.[3]
  • 2026-09-07Prime Minister Macut requested the president to dissolve parliament, formalizing early general elections.[4]
  • 2026-09-14The university student movement, which had led protests for approximately two years, submitted an electoral list of candidates and officially entered the election race.[5]
  • 2026-09-27President Vučić resigned to run for the prime ministership, and National Assembly Speaker Brnabić stepped in as acting president the following day.[6][7]

Public Trends

The university student-led anti-corruption movement continued for about two years starting in November 2024, demanding early general elections, the rule of law, and accountability. The March 2025 protest exceeded 100,000 participants even by government figures, and clashes with police occurred in May 2026. The student movement participated in the October 25 general election with an independent candidate list in September 2026.

Discrepancies in Figures

Participants in the Belgrade protest on 2025-03-15: Official figure from the Ministry of Internal Affairs was 107,000. The independent monitoring group 'Archive of Public Gatherings (Arhiv javnih skupova)' estimated 275,000 to 325,000, which is approximately 168,000 to 218,000 higher than the official figure.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StatePeter Pellegrini2024-06Independent (Former leader of Hlas-SD)
Head of GovernmentRobert Fico2023-10Smer–Social Democracy (Smer-SD)-led coalition

Reference date 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Prior Trajectory

Following the inauguration of the fourth Fico government in October 2023, military aid to Ukraine was suspended in January 2024 and restructuring of public broadcaster RTVS commenced. On May 15, 2024, Prime Minister Fico was shot and seriously wounded in Handlová. Subsequently, amendments to the penal code and the easing of penalties related to corruption ensued.

Direction of the Current Government

Externally, it maintains a critical stance toward EU sanctions against Russia and opposes Ukraine's NATO accession. Domestically, it is pivoting toward strengthening state authority, including explicitly specifying 'sovereignty of national identity in cultural and ethical matters' via a constitutional amendment in September 2025, and replacing the independent Whistleblower Protection Office with a government-controlled agency in December 2025.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2024-05-15Prime Minister Fico was shot and seriously wounded after a government meeting in Handlová.[1]
  • 2024-12Biweekly anti-government protests began following Prime Minister Fico's visit to Moscow and meeting with Putin.[2]
  • 2025-02-07The largest anti-government protests since 2018 were held across 41 domestic locations and 13 overseas cities.[3]
  • 2025-09-26Parliament passed a constitutional amendment with 90 votes recognizing 'only two sexes, male and female' and affirming national sovereignty over cultural and ethical matters.[4]
  • 2025-11-17Tens of thousands protested across dozens of localities against the abolition of the Velvet Revolution Day public holiday (under the pretext of austerity), and a student chalk-graffiti protest ('Chalk Revolution') spread.[5][6]
  • 2025-12-09Parliament passed legislation abolishing and replacing the independent Whistleblower Protection Office with 78 votes.[7]
  • 2025-12-15Approximately 7,000 people protested in Bratislava against the restructuring of the whistleblower system and amendments to the penal code.[8]
  • 2026-09-18Prime Minister Fico visited Ukraine.[9]

Public Trends

Biweekly protests opposing the pro-Russian foreign policy stance and legislation concerning the rule of law continued from December 2024, expanding to tens of thousands in February and November 2025. Participation of youth and students was observed, as seen in the 'Chalk Revolution' initiated by high school students in November 2025. No reports of large-scale protests in 2026 were identifiable within the verified scope (news agency and regional media searches).

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateKonstantinos Tasoulas2025-03-13New Democracy (ND), elected by Parliament
Head of GovernmentKyriakos Mitsotakis2019-07New Democracy (ND)

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

After taking power in 2019, the Mitsotakis government was re-elected in 2023 and has maintained a single-party majority government. Following the Tempi train crash on February 28, 2023 (57 dead, many of them university students), responsibility for railway safety management, including signaling systems and personnel shortages, became a political issue. In February 2025, parliament elected former parliamentary speaker Tasoulas, the government's candidate, as president.

Current Government Direction

The government is maintaining its approach of resolving responsibility for the Tempi crash through judicial procedures (trial of 36 defendants) and parliamentary investigations. In October 2025, management authority over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier area in front of the parliament building was transferred to the Ministry of National Defence, shifting toward restricting rallies in that area. In September 2026, labor union rallies concerning living costs were held at the time of the economic address at the Thessaloniki International Fair.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-02-12Parliament elected Tasoulas as president with 160 out of 300 votes (inaugurated on March 13).[1]
  • 2025-02-28On the 2nd anniversary of the Tempi crash, hundreds of thousands protested across more than 300 cities, accompanied by general strikes across aviation, rail, and maritime transport.[2]
  • 2025-03-07A motion of no confidence submitted by four opposition parties was rejected by 136 votes in favor to 157 against.[3]
  • 2025-10-22Following a 23-day hunger strike by Panos Routsis, a relative of a victim, an amendment transferring jurisdiction over the area in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier to the Ministry of National Defence was put to a parliamentary vote.[4][5]
  • 2026-02-28On the 3rd anniversary of the Tempi crash, memorial and condemnation rallies were held nationwide, including in Athens, Thessaloniki, and Larissa.[6]
  • 2026-03-23In Larissa, the trial for the Tempi crash began for 36 defendants, including railway officials, Ministry of Transport personnel, and Hellenic Train executives.[7]
  • 2026-09-05On the day of the Prime Minister's Thessaloniki economic speech, over 25,000 people (police estimate) protested over wage increases and cost-of-living issues.[2]

Public Trends

Tempi crash-related protests were repeated on a nationwide scale on every anniversary through 2025–2026, with victims' families, labor unions, and student organizations participating under the slogan 'Not an accident, but murder.' In September 2026, labor rallies focusing on living costs and wages took place in Thessaloniki. In September 2026, 2025 protest footage was recirculated on social media with claims of 'Greece paralyzed,' becoming the subject of fact-checking.

Data Caution

The Tempi trial is expected to take approximately two years, and the parliamentary inquiry into political responsibility is proceeding separately.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateAndrás Baka2026-08-19Elected by Parliament (2026-08-11)
Head of GovernmentPéter Magyar2026-05-09Tisza (Respect and Freedom Party)

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Fidesz held power for 16 years starting in 2010, restructuring the judicial, media, and constitutional systems, while the EU had frozen funds allocated to Hungary citing rule-of-law and corruption issues. In 2025, a law banning LGBTQ+ events was implemented under the pretext of 'child protection.'

Current Government Direction

The Magyar government, having won a two-thirds majority in the April 2026 general election, is pivoting toward institutional restructuring aligned with EU standards, including judicial reform, the establishment of an anti-corruption investigative agency, a 12-year term limit for lawmakers, and accession to the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO). More than 100 laws were amended to unfreeze approximately €16.4 billion in frozen EU funds, and the president elected under the Orbán government was replaced following a constitutional amendment in July 2026.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-06-28Despite the government's ban on the event, the Budapest Pride march took place as a city hall-hosted event.[1]
  • 2026-04-12In the general election, the Tisza Party won 53.18% on the party list and 141 out of 199 seats, securing a constitution-amending majority, while Fidesz won 52 seats and Our Homeland Movement won 6 seats.[2]
  • 2026-05-09Magyar took office as Prime Minister and demanded the resignation of senior officials from the Orbán government era by May 31.[3]
  • 2026-05-29The EU agreed on a plan to unfreeze approximately €16 billion in Hungarian funds conditional on implementing anti-corruption and rule-of-law reforms (a deadline of August 31 for €10 billion of the recovery fund).[4]
  • 2026-07-14Parliament passed a constitutional amendment including the dismissal of President Tamás Sulyok by 139 votes in favor and 6 against (Fidesz lawmakers abstained/did not attend).[5]
  • 2026-07-20President Sulyok's term ended, and Parliamentary Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer assumed the duties of acting president.[6]
  • 2026-08-11Parliament elected András Baka as president, and he took office on August 19.[7]
  • 2026-08-31The government announced that it had satisfied all 27 core milestones and over 100 detailed milestones required to receive the €10 billion recovery fund.[8]

Public Trends

The June 2025 Budapest Pride march drew an estimated 180,000–200,000 participants (organizer estimates), showing large-scale civil disobedience against government bans. In the April 2026 general election, the Tisza Party recorded the highest vote share since the transition of the regime, and a rally to 'celebrate the systemic transition' was scheduled in front of the parliament building on inauguration day. Following the change in government, no large-scale anti-government protests were reported within the monitored scope (wire agencies and Euronews coverage).

Numerical Discrepancy

General election results: Early ballot counting reports (BTA, 2026-04-13) reported 138 seats for Tisza and 55 seats for Fidesz, but the National Election Office final result was 141 seats for Tisza and 52 seats for Fidesz; the final official figures serve as the baseline. 2025 Pride participants: 180,000–200,000 according to organizers, with no independently verified figures.

Data Caution

One constituency in Vas County became subject to judicial review following challenges over candidate nominations bearing the same name.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateFelipe VI2014-06Constitutional Monarch
Head of GovernmentPedro Sánchez2018-06Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE)–Sumar coalition, lacking parliamentary majority

As of 2026-10-07 · Compiled from open sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

The Sánchez administration has pursued legislation as a minority coalition reliant on external support from Catalan parties (ERC, Junts), among others. In June 2025, Santos Cerdán, the party's organizational secretary, resigned over allegations of public contract kickbacks, prompting the Prime Minister to apologize while declaring there would be no general election before 2027. Rising housing costs have persisted, with rents roughly doubling on average over the past decade.

Current Government Direction

Following an eviction incident in September 2026, the government attempted a policy pivot toward strengthened tenant protections via royal decrees (decreto-ley), introducing eviction protection for vulnerable tenants through 2030, regulations on short-term and room rentals, a ban on residential purchases by speculative funds through 2028, and automatic lease renewals. However, on October 2, Congress rejected both royal decrees, and the Prime Minister was reported to be considering whether to call an early general election.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-04-05The first coordinated housing protests across 40 cities took place under the slogan 'End the housing business.'[1]
  • 2025-06-12Santos Cerdán, PSOE organizational secretary, resigned from party posts and his parliamentary seat over allegations of illegal commissions amounting to €620,000.[2]
  • 2026-09-23In Madrid's Retiro district, 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, who had resided there for over 70 years, was evicted after her rent increased from €500 to €2,650 per month.[3]
  • 2026-09-27Following an anti-eviction march in Madrid, an encampment began at Puerta del Sol.[4][5]
  • 2026-09-29The cabinet approved two housing royal decrees encompassing eviction protections, rent regulations, and automatic lease renewals.[6]
  • 2026-10-02The Congress of Deputies rejected the housing decree 178 to 172 and the automatic renewal decree 184 to 166, with opposition from PP, Vox, Junts, and UPN.[7][8]
  • 2026-10-03Prime Minister Sánchez was reported to be reviewing whether to call an early general election, while the leader of the far-right Vox demanded early elections.[8]

Public Trends

Following simultaneous protests across 40 cities in April 2025, housing issues established themselves as a primary collective action agenda. Triggered by the eviction of an elderly resident in September 2026, an encampment drew comparisons to the 2011 '15-M' movement at Puerta del Sol in Madrid, with protests also taking place at Plaça de Catalunya in Barcelona. Demonstrators successfully blocked another eviction in Madrid, forcing its postponement to October 14.

Discrepancies in Figures

Participants in the 2026-09-27 Madrid march: Government Delegation (Delegación del Gobierno) official estimate of approximately 25,000; Tenants' Union (Sindicato de Inquilinas) claim of 300,000 (12 times the official figure); Reuters report of approximately 30,000. Housing shortage estimates: Bank of Spain estimates were cited differently across reports, at approximately 550,000 units (NPR) and 750,000 units (Reuters).

Data Caution

The central bank's housing shortage estimates are cited differently across media reports depending on the calculation date, requiring verification of source data.

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of StateEmmanuel Macron2017-05 (Re-elected 2022-05, next presidential election 2027)Renaissance centrist camp
Head of GovernmentSébastien Lecornu2025-09 (Reappointed 2025-10-10)Renaissance, minority government without parliamentary majority

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the list of sources below.

Previous Trajectory

Following the 2024 snap legislative election, a 'hung parliament' with no majority was formed, leading to a succession of prime ministers. The Barnier cabinet collapsed in December 2024 following a vote of no confidence (331 votes) while attempting to pass the social security budget via Article 49.3 of the Constitution, and the Bayrou cabinet stepped down after losing a confidence vote on September 8, 2025. The 2023 pension reform (raising retirement age from 62 to 64) remained a continuous target of opposition protests.

Current Government's Direction

Amid threats of a no-confidence vote by the Socialist Party in October 2025, the Lecornu government pivoted toward postponing the retirement age increase from the 2023 pension reform until January 2028. The 2026 budget was adopted in February 2026 following the invocation of Article 49.3 and the rejection of a no-confidence motion. The 2027 budget bill submitted in October 2026 is oriented toward austerity, aiming to reduce the fiscal deficit to 5% of GDP through €54 billion in spending cuts, a civil service wage freeze, and caps on pension indexation.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2024-12-04The National Assembly passed a no-confidence motion against the Barnier government with 331 votes.[1]
  • 2025-09-08Prime Minister Bayrou lost a vote of confidence in the National Assembly with 194 votes in favor and 364 against, announcing his intention to resign.[2]
  • 2025-09-10An estimated 175,000 people according to the Ministry of the Interior participated in the nationwide 'Bloquons tout' action, and over 470 people were arrested.[3]
  • 2025-09-18Union-led nationwide strikes and protests took place, demanding the withdrawal of budget cuts and the taxation of the wealthy.[4]
  • 2025-10-10Prime Minister Lecornu was reappointed by President Macron four days after his resignation.[5]
  • 2025-10-14Prime Minister Lecornu announced a suspension of the retirement age hike until January 2028.[6]
  • 2026-01-19Prime Minister Lecornu announced the invocation of Article 49.3 of the Constitution to pass the 2026 budget, which aimed to maintain a deficit of 5% of GDP.[9]
  • 2026-02-02The left-wing no-confidence motion was rejected with 260 votes (289 required), virtually confirming the adoption of the 2026 budget.[7]
  • 2026-10-01The government announced the 2027 budget bill targeting €54 billion in cuts and a 5% deficit (public debt at approximately 120% of GDP).[8]

Public Trends

In September 2025, decentralized civic actions under 'Bloquons tout' and general strikes by labor unions continued over austerity and pension issues. In October 2026, ahead of the announcement of the 2027 budget bill, public sector strikes opposing wage freezes occurred, with left-wing parties and unions characterizing the budget bill as 'austerity'.

Numerical Discrepancies

2025-09-10 protests: Interior Ministry official figure approx. 175,000, CGT union approx. 250,000 (discrepancy of approx. 75,000). 2025-09-18 protests: Interior Ministry official figure over 450,000 outside Paris + 55,000 in Paris (approx. 500,000), CGT over 1 million (approx. 2-fold difference).

PositionNameTook OfficeAffiliation
Head of StateFrank-Walter Steinmeier2017-03 (Re-elected 2022-02)From the Social Democratic Party (SPD)
Head of GovernmentFriedrich Merz2025-05-06Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU)–SPD coalition

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the list of sources below.

Previous Trajectory

Following the collapse of the Scholz traffic light coalition, in the February 2025 snap federal election, the CDU/CSU took first place with 28.5%, and the AfD surpassed 20% to take second place. Merz fell six votes short of a majority in the first round of voting in the Bundestag in May 2025, but was elected chancellor in the second round on the same day with 325 votes. After two consecutive years of negative growth, the German economy grew by 0.2% in 2025.

Current Government's Direction

The Merz government is pivoting toward fiscal expansion and rearmament with a €500 billion infrastructure investment fund over 12 years, increased defense spending, and subsidies for industrial energy prices. Under the Military Service Modernization Act implemented in January 2026, it is pursuing troop expansion (targeting 260,000 active-duty personnel by 2035), including mandatory military service questionnaires for 18-year-old men. Concurrently, friction with labor groups persists over reforms in pensions, working hours, and healthcare.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-02-23In the snap federal election, CDU/CSU garnered 28.5%, AfD over 20%, and SPD 16.4%.[1]
  • 2025-05-06After failing in the first round with 310 votes, Merz was elected chancellor in the second round with 325 votes.[1]
  • 2026-01The Military Service Modernization Act took effect, making military service survey responses mandatory for 18-year-old men.[6]
  • 2026-01-28The government lowered its 2026 growth forecast from 1.3% to approximately 1%.[2]
  • 2026-09-06In the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election, the AfD came in first with 43.8% (39 of 83 seats), while the CDU obtained 17.2%.[3]
  • 2026-09-20In the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election, the AfD ranked first with 38.2% and the CDU recorded 4.9%, while on the same day in the Berlin election, The Left (Die Linke) took first place with 25.7%.[4]
  • 2026-09-26The DGB trade union confederation held rallies opposing cuts to pensions and social security across 15 cities, while on the same day anti-conscription protests by students took place in approximately 100 cities.[5][6]

Public Trends

On September 26, 2026, union-led rallies against social security cuts and student-led protests against the military service law took place simultaneously nationwide. In elections, votes abandoning the federal governing coalition (CDU and SPD) flowed in both directions, with the AfD winning the most votes in two eastern states and The Left placing first in Berlin.

Numerical Discrepancies

2026-09-26 DGB rallies: Organizers reported a total of 175,000 across 15 cities; police counts varied by city from 5,500 in Berlin to 25,000 in Nuremberg, with no verifiable official total. Anti-conscription student protests on the same day: Organizers reported approx. 45,000, while police reported lower figures, including approx. 2,400 in Berlin.

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of StateCharles III2022-09Constitutional Monarch
Head of GovernmentAndy Burnham2026-07-20Labour Party, House of Commons majority

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

The Keir Starmer Labour government, which came to power in the July 2024 general election, trailed the right-wing Reform UK in opinion polls amid successive policy reversals and low approval ratings. Following the May 2026 local and regional elections in which Labour lost approximately 1,200 seats and fell to 9 seats in the Welsh Parliament (Senedd), Prime Minister Starmer announced his resignation on June 22, 2026.

Current Government Direction

The Burnham administration has made growth, regional devolution, and addressing the cost of living its priorities, reversing the Starmer government's £1.8 billion digital ID card project. It is pivoting toward a cost-of-living and region-centric direction by cutting VAT on energy bills, restoring the £2 bus fare cap, slashing business rates by 20% for pubs and music venues, establishing a Manchester-based 'Prime Minister's Office of the North', and overhauling vocational education, while concurrently pursuing conditional welfare reform to curb welfare spending.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-09-13The 'Unite the Kingdom' march organized by right-wing activist Tommy Robinson took place in London, with police estimating 110,000 to 150,000 participants, leaving 26 police officers injured.[1][2]
  • 2026-05-07In the local elections, Reform UK gained more than 1,200 seats on English local councils, while in the Welsh Parliament, Plaid Cymru secured 43 seats, Reform 34 seats, and Labour 9 seats.[3]
  • 2026-06-22Prime Minister Starmer announced his resignation amid a loss of support among Labour MPs.[4]
  • 2026-07-14Burnham secured succession as party leader as the sole candidate after receiving endorsements from 349 Labour MPs.[5]
  • 2026-07-20Burnham took office as Prime Minister following an audience with the King.[6]
  • 2026-07-28A Survation poll showed Labour leading Reform UK at 26% to 24%, marking the first Labour lead in over a year (YouGov reported a 22% tie).[7]

Public Trends

The September 2025 right-wing rally in London was massive, with police estimating over 100,000 participants, leading to clashes with an anti-racism counter-protest (approximately 5,000 participants). Electively, the May 2026 local elections saw votes shift toward Reform UK and the Welsh nationalist party Plaid Cymru. Since Burnham took office in 2026, no large-scale collective street action has been reported within the verified scope (wire services and UK media coverage).

Discrepancies in Figures

2025-09-13 'Unite the Kingdom' attendees: Metropolitan Police official estimate was 110,000–150,000. Organizer Tommy Robinson claimed on social media that 'police estimated 3 million', but fact-checking organization Full Fact determined this to be untrue (approximately 20 to 27 times the official figure).

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTenure StartAffiliation
Head of StateKarol Nawrocki2025-08-06Independent (supported by Law and Justice [PiS])
Head of GovernmentDonald Tusk2023-12Civic Coalition (KO)-led pro-EU coalition

As of 2026-10-07 · Collected from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the source list below.

Previous Trajectory

The Tusk coalition government, established after the 2023 parliamentary election, has been pursuing the restoration of the rule of law—rolling back judicial reforms from the PiS government era—and strengthening EU cooperation. In the presidential runoff on June 1, 2025, PiS-backed candidate Nawrocki defeated pro-government candidate Trzaskowski with 50.89% of the vote, and Prime Minister Tusk confirmed coalition unity via a vote of confidence.

Current Government Direction

In a 'cohabitation' framework where the president and government belong to opposing camps, the president continues to exercise veto power over judicial reforms, EU defense loans, Digital Services implementation, and crypto-asset regulations. The government carried out a restructuring in July 2025 by establishing the Ministry of Energy and expanding the economic authority of the Minister of Finance, and in defense, is expanding procurement (selecting Sweden for the Orka submarine program). Following the president's veto of the SAFE loan bill in March 2026, the government is securing rearmament financing via state development bank borrowing authorized by cabinet resolution. According to preliminary GUS estimates, real GDP growth in 2025 was 3.6%.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-06-01Nawrocki was elected with 50.89% in the presidential runoff.[1][2]
  • 2025-07Prime Minister Tusk reshuffled the cabinet, including the creation of the Ministry of Energy.[1]
  • 2025-08-06President Nawrocki took office.[3]
  • 2025-09-10A formation of Russian drones entered Polish airspace, prompting fighter jets to scramble (evaluated as an unprecedented event in modern Polish history).[1]
  • 2025-11-13Marshal of the Sejm Szymon Hołownia resigned, and Włodzimierz Czarzasty succeeded him five days later.[1]
  • 2026-01-30The Central Statistical Office (GUS) released preliminary figures indicating a 3.6% real GDP growth rate for 2025 (3.0% in 2024).[8]
  • 2026-02-01President Nawrocki defended his use of the veto, citing a record of signing 132 bills and vetoing 20 since taking office.[4]
  • 2026-03-12President Nawrocki vetoed a bill to borrow €43.7 billion under the EU defense loan program (SAFE), citing sovereignty constraints stemming from foreign currency-denominated long-term debt and EU conditional enforcement.[6]
  • 2026-03-13The government adopted a cabinet resolution to take out the SAFE loan in the name of the Armed Forces Support Fund through the state development bank (BGK), and the presidential office referred to a Constitutional Tribunal review, calling it a 'circumvention of the law.'[7]
  • 2026-06-12President Nawrocki exercised his 37th veto, surpassing the all-time record for a president (previously 35 vetoes over 10 years by Kwaśniewski).[3]

Public Trends

The 2025 presidential election runoff was decided by a narrow margin of 50.89% to 49.11%. In a November 2025 survey, 32.1% of respondents answered that they wanted the emergence of a new political party, and the far-right 'Confederation of the Polish Crown' (Braun) approached a 10% approval rating. Large-scale street collective actions in 2026 could not be confirmed within the verification scope (Polish public service and English-language media reports).

Data Caveats

Credit rating agencies pointed out that the deadlock between the president and the government burdens fiscal stability and policymaking capacity (citing Notes from Poland).

4. Current Status Briefing

PositionNameTerm StartAffiliation
Head of State (President)Sergio Mattarella2015-02 (Re-elected in 2022)Independent
Head of Government (Prime Minister)Giorgia Meloni2022-10Right-wing coalition led by Brothers of Italy (FdI) (Lega, Forza Italia, etc.)

Base date 2026-10-07 · Gathered from public sources. Footnote numbers correspond to the list of sources below.

Previous Trajectory

The Meloni government has been in power with a right-wing coalition since taking office in October 2022, and entered the EU's Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) in 2024. It pursued a judicial reform constitutional amendment led by Justice Minister Carlo Nordio (separation of careers for judges and prosecutors, split and lottery system for the High Council of the Judiciary, establishment of a separate disciplinary court), but it was rejected in a March 2026 referendum.

Direction of Current Government

Following the rejection of the judicial constitutional amendment, the government shifted its direction toward electoral system reform combining proportional representation with a majority bonus; the Chamber of Deputies passed the reform bill in July 2026, which is now awaiting a vote in the Senate. On the fiscal front, with the 2025 deficit confirmed at 3.1% of GDP, the finance minister commented that exiting the EDP could be delayed to 2027, and the 2027 budget proposal is expected to include income tax bracket adjustments. While the possibility of early general elections in April 2027 before the expiration of the term in September 2027 was reported, no official decision has been made.

Chronology 2024–2026

  • 2025-10-03A one-day general strike and rallies protesting the seizure of the Gaza aid convoy (Global Sumud Flotilla) were held in over 100 cities (estimated over 2 million participants by CGIL).[4]
  • 2026-03-02Istat announced provisional figures of 0.5% GDP growth for 2025 and a fiscal deficit of 3.1% of GDP (3.4% in 2024).[8]
  • 2026-03-23The judicial reform referendum (March 23–24) was held with a turnout of approximately 59%, failing with approximately 54% voting against and 46% voting in favor.[1][2]
  • 2026-03-24Prime Minister Meloni accepted the result and stated she would continue her term, while opposition Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein declared the establishment of an alternative coalition.[2][3]
  • 2026-06-23Bloomberg reported that Prime Minister Meloni consulted with the presidential office while considering early general elections in April 2027.[6]
  • 2026-07-16The Chamber of Deputies passed a majority-bonus proportional representation electoral bill allocating an additional 70 seats in the Chamber and 35 seats in the Senate to a coalition winning 42% or more of the vote.[5]
  • 2026-09-22Istat confirmed the 2025 deficit at 3.1%, leaving Italy subject to the EU Excessive Deficit Procedure.[7]

Public Trends

On October 3, 2025, a general strike over the Gaza issue paralyzed transportation and schools, with approximately 300,000 marching in Rome and 100,000 in Milan, and minor clashes occurring in some cities. The March 2026 judicial reform referendum recorded approximately 59% turnout, with 'No' votes prevailing in 14 regions, including the South. In opinion polls, Roberto Vannacci's newly formed far-right party 'Futuro Nazionale' was reported to have garnered 6–7% support.

Numerical Discrepancies

① October 3, 2025 general strike participants: The union (CGIL) claimed over 2 million participants; government tallies such as the Ministry of the Interior could not be confirmed. ② 2025 fiscal indicators: Istat's provisional March figures (growth rate 0.5%, debt ratio 137.1%, tax-to-GDP ratio 43.1%) differ from the finalized September figures (growth rate 0.6%, debt ratio 136.7%, tax-to-GDP ratio 42.9%), while the deficit remains identical at 3.1% — based on finalized figures.

Data Caveats

The outcome of the Senate vote on the electoral reform bill and whether early general elections will occur remain unconfirmed as of October 7, 2026. 2024 events (European Parliament elections, etc.) could not be included in the timeline due to search constraints.
